Compile

kum-PYL -- built from 'com-' (together) plus a root related to gathering or heaping. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To compile to collect information from different sources and arrange it in a single, organized form.

Before the trial, lawyers had to compile thousands of pages of evidence into a single binder.

Worked Example

A librarian gathers hundreds of scattered newspaper clippings, letters, and photographs from an entire century and organizes them into one carefully indexed digital archive.

That careful gathering and organizing of scattered pieces into one complete whole is exactly what compile means. Unlike 'scatter,' which spreads things apart, compile brings them together.

How Compile Sits Among Its Neighbors

Antonyms

disperse

How Strong Is It? — gather → assemble → compile

gather vs. compile

gather vs. compile: Gather is a more everyday, general word than compile -- gather can describe collecting almost anything, while compile specifically implies organizing collected information into a finished, structured form.

assemble vs. compile

assemble vs. compile: Assemble can feel more deliberate than compile in some contexts: compile often focuses on gathering information or data, while assemble can suggest carefully fitting separate pieces together into a complete structure.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — com-

prefix — com-: together (Latin)

root — -pile

root — -pile: to heap, pack together (Latin (compilare))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin compilare meant 'to plunder' or 'heap together,' built from com- ('together') and pilare, related to piling things up. To compile something, at its root, is to heap scattered pieces together into one organized pile -- the same root that gives us compilation.
